summary: A progress report from Rand on checking which ARPANET sites had been tested against the early protocols. The table notes whether each host handled the host-host protocol basics, the initial connection protocol, and Telnet as user and server. It warns that these were one-time arranged tests, not a measure of ongoing availability.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card showing which computers passed a few simple tests so far. The teacher warns that passing one test does not mean the computer is always working.

questions: what was the arpanet network checkout
what does ncp-107 mean in rfc 214
subtitle: A 1971 status table of which ARPANET hosts had passed basic protocol checks.

tldr.problem: Sites joining the ARPANET needed to know which other hosts actually worked with the early protocols.
tldr.mechanism: Rand tabulated, per host, whether the NCP, the initial connection protocol, user and server Telnet, the logger and an access service had been verified, with comments on failures.
tldr.outcome: The author warns that these were arranged one-time tests that show no continuous availability, and says the RFC would be updated in about one month.

today: This is a dated status report from August 1971 and says nothing about how those hosts work now. Its metadata says it obsoletes RFC 193 and RFC 198, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it.

sections.title: The Checkout Table
sections.content:
As of August 21, 1971, the author had performed verifications with the sites listed. A mark of x means a function was verified, a blank means it was not verified, na means it does not apply to the host, and ? means a comment follows. The columns are NCP-107, ICP-156, user Telnet, server Telnet, Logger and Access Service.

Eleven rows are listed, from UCLA Sigma7 to LINCOLN /67. For UTAH the entry says only that TENEX was being installed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer gets a row of check marks for the tests it passed. An empty box means nobody tried yet.

sections.title: What the Checks Prove
sections.content:
The author says the 'NCP-107' heading is somewhat misleading. It does not mean a thorough check of all the functions in Document 1 and RFC 107. It only means the NCP answered a RESET, which the Rand NCP needs before it considers a remote host up, and did what an initial connection needed.

Functions such as ECHO, Give Back and error message generation were not checked, except some with UCSB and SDC, and not exhaustively. BBN was writing a protocol certifier for its DDP-516 host to do this automatically. The tests were arranged and show no degree of continuous availability.
sections.plainLanguage: One check mark only means a computer answered the door and said hello. It does not mean everything inside works.

sections.title: Comments on Problem Hosts
sections.content:
Three comments are given. At SRI NIC, a server Telnet and logger exist but do not process Telnet messages correctly. At MIT Multics, only an interim logger could be reached, and it sent a 'ts' message. At SDC, the logger crashes the system after login.

Discrepancies were to be reported by phone, and the RFC would be updated in about one month.
sections.plainLanguage: A few computers had problems, like one that crashed after someone logged in. The author asks to be told by phone about any mistakes.

references.text: RFC 107, cited by the report as describing the NCP functions (title not given in the text).
